usage: 제가 대접할게요
Let me treat you (to a meal)
Said when you want to pay and host; warmer and more formal than just 제가 살게요.
잘 대접받았어요
I was treated really well / hosted generously
Passive 대접받다 = to be treated/hosted; common thank-you after visiting someone's home.
examples: 집에 초대해서 한정식으로 대접했어요.
I invited them over and hosted them with a Korean set meal.
한정식 = traditional Korean course meal; 대접하다 implies you put real effort into hosting.
손님을 이렇게 대접하면 안 되죠.
You shouldn't treat a customer like this.
Also used for service quality — 대접하다 covers how you treat people, not just feeding them.
오늘은 제가 대접하는 거니까 편하게 드세요.
It's my treat today, so eat comfortably.
Natural host phrase at a restaurant when you're picking up the bill.
nuance: 대접하다 is warmer and more deliberate than 사다 (to buy a meal): it implies hosting and showing respect, often by serving food at home or treating someone older or a guest. It also describes how you treat people in general (손님 대접 = treating someone like a guest). The passive 대접받다 is just as common as the active form.
mistakes: Using 대접하다 for a casual 'I'll get this coffee' — for small, casual treats just say 제가 살게요; save 대접하다 for proper hosting or respectful treatment.

english: to help out / to lend a hand
usage: 내가 거들어 줄게
I'll give you a hand
Offering to pitch in on a hands-on task like carrying or cleaning up.
좀 거들어 줄래?
Can you help out a bit?
Casual request to a friend or family member to lend a hand with chores.
examples: 이삿짐 옮기는 거 거들어 줄게요.
I'll help out moving the boxes.
거들다 fits physical helping-out; very natural for moving day among friends.
엄마 설거지 좀 거들어.
Help your mom with the dishes a bit.
거들다 = chip in on a task someone else is already doing, rather than doing it for them.
옆에서 말로만 거들지 말고 직접 좀 해.
Stop just chiming in from the side and actually do it yourself.
거들다 can also mean to add words/back someone up — here 'chiming in' without acting.
nuance: 거들다 means to assist with something already in progress — to pitch in or lend a hand, often on physical or household tasks. It's lighter than 돕다 (to help) and implies you're a secondary helper, not the main doer. Note the ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ (거듭니다), but stays elsewhere (거들어요, 거들 거예요).
mistakes: Writing the formal form as 거들습니다 — the ㄹ drops, so it's 거듭니다.
Treating 거들다 as full help; for serious help or rescue use 돕다, not 거들다.

usage: 자리 좀 양보해 주세요
Please give up your seat
Asking someone to offer a seat — often to an elderly or pregnant passenger on the subway.
이번엔 내가 양보할게
I'll let it go / give in this time
Conceding in a disagreement to keep the peace; very common in relationships.
examples: 지하철에서 할머니께 자리를 양보했어요.
I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
Classic 양보 scene; 께 is the honorific marker for the older person.
서로 한 발씩 양보하면 좋잖아.
It's nice if we each give a little, right?
한 발씩 양보하다 = 'each take a step back / compromise', a set expression.
운전할 때 양보 운전 좀 해.
Drive courteously and yield a bit.
양보 운전 = defensive/courteous driving, letting others merge — useful road vocab.
nuance: 양보하다 covers both physical yielding (a seat, the right of way) and figurative conceding (backing down in an argument, letting someone have their way). It carries a positive, courteous nuance — yielding is seen as considerate, not weak. The bare noun 양보 appears everywhere on signs and in driving etiquette.
mistakes: Confusing 양보하다 (yield/concede) with 포기하다 (give up entirely) — 양보 is giving way to someone, not abandoning a goal.

usage: 배웅 안 나와도 돼
You don't have to come see me off
Politely telling a host not to walk you out; 나오다 = come out (to the door/gate).
공항까지 배웅했어요
I saw them off all the way to the airport
Seeing someone off before a flight; shows you cared enough to go far.
examples: 친구가 떠나는 게 아쉬워서 역까지 배웅했어.
I was sad my friend was leaving, so I saw them off at the station.
배웅하다 = accompany someone leaving to the door/station; warm farewell gesture.
할머니가 문 앞까지 나와서 배웅해 주셨어요.
Grandma came out to the door to see me off.
Common Korean courtesy — older hosts walk guests out; -아/어 주시다 shows the kindness done for you.
다음에 또 와, 하면서 배웅해 줬어요.
They saw me off saying 'come again next time.'
Natural parting scene after visiting someone's home.
nuance: 배웅하다 is the counterpart to 마중하다 (meeting an arrival): it means accompanying someone who is leaving — walking them to the door, station, or airport. It signals warmth and respect, and declining a host's 배웅 ('배웅 안 나오셔도 돼요') is itself polite. The noun 배웅 is used freely (배웅 나가다, 배웅 인사).
mistakes: Swapping 배웅하다 (see off / departure) with 마중하다 (meet / arrival) — they're opposites; mixing them up is a classic learner error.

usage: 새해를 맞이해서
To welcome / on the occasion of the new year
Very common set phrase opening greetings, sales, and announcements.
따뜻하게 맞이해 주셨어요
They welcomed me warmly
Said about a host or company that received you kindly.
examples: 사장님이 직접 나와서 손님을 맞이했어요.
The owner came out personally to welcome the guests.
맞이하다 = receive/greet someone arriving; a bit more formal and warm than just 만나다.
새해를 맞이해서 가족끼리 떡국을 먹었어요.
To welcome the new year, my family ate rice-cake soup together.
N을/를 맞이해서 = 'on the occasion of / to welcome N'; fixed pattern for holidays and events.
곧 30대를 맞이하는 기분이 묘해요.
It feels strange to be about to enter my 30s.
맞이하다 also marks reaching a new stage of life — useful and relatable in your late 20s.
nuance: 맞이하다 means to welcome or receive — both people (greeting an arriving guest) and occasions (a new year, a new phase of life). For greeting guests it overlaps with 마중하다 but sounds warmer and more formal; for events, 새해를/명절을 맞이하다 is a fixed expression you'll see constantly. The everyday spoken cousin is 맞다 ('손님 맞을 준비'), but 맞이하다 is the clearer dictionary verb.
mistakes: Confusing 맞이하다 (welcome/receive) with 맞추다 (to fit/match/set) — different verbs despite the similar look.

english: to break / to violate (a rule or promise)
usage: 약속을 어기다
to break a promise
The single most common collocation; failing to keep your word.
규칙을 어기면 안 돼요
You mustn't break the rules
규칙/법/신호 등을 어기다 = to violate rules/laws/signals.
examples: 또 약속을 어겨서 친구가 화났어.
I broke my promise again, so my friend got angry.
약속을 어기다 is the go-to phrase for letting someone down by not keeping your word.
신호를 어기고 건너면 위험해요.
It's dangerous to cross against the signal.
신호를 어기다 = ignore/run a traffic signal; practical safety vocab.
회사 규정을 어기면 불이익이 있어요.
If you break company rules, there are penalties.
규정을 어기다 = violate regulations; 불이익 = disadvantage/penalty, common workplace word.
nuance: 어기다 is the standard verb for breaking something intangible you're bound to keep — a promise (약속), a rule (규칙), a law (법), or a signal (신호). It's the direct antonym of 지키다 (to keep/abide by). Don't use it for physically breaking objects; that's 깨다 or 부수다.
mistakes: Using 어기다 for breaking a physical object — for cups/phones use 깨다/고장 내다; 어기다 is only for rules, promises, and laws.

english: to keep / to protect / to abide by
usage: 약속 꼭 지켜
Be sure to keep your promise
The opposite of 약속을 어기다; demanding someone follow through.
거리 좀 지켜 주세요
Please keep your distance
거리를/순서를/규칙을 지키다 = keep distance/order/rules; very common request.
examples: 나는 약속은 무조건 지켜.
I always keep my promises no matter what.
약속을 지키다 = keep one's word; 무조건 = unconditionally/no matter what.
줄 설 때 순서 좀 지켜 주세요.
Please follow the order when lining up.
순서를 지키다 = wait your turn / keep the order; handy in any Korean queue.
비밀 꼭 지켜 줄 수 있어?
Can you definitely keep this a secret?
비밀을 지키다 = keep a secret; everyday trust vocabulary among friends.
nuance: 지키다 is a high-frequency verb spanning three senses: keep (a promise, a secret, a time), abide by (rules, order, distance), and protect/guard (a person, a place). It's the direct antonym of 어기다 for rules and promises. Note that 지키지 마세요 ('don't keep it') is rarely needed in real life — the natural negative is usually 어기지 마세요.
mistakes: Saying 약속을 가지다 for 'keep a promise' — the verb is 지키다; 가지다 means physically have/hold.

english: to show kindness / to be generous
usage: 은혜를 베풀다
to show kindness / do someone a favor
은혜/호의/친절을 베풀다 = bestow a kindness; slightly formal, heartfelt tone.
한턱 베풀어
Treat us / be generous (and pay)
Playful way to ask someone to treat the group, like when they got good news.
examples: 사장님이 직원들한테 항상 잘 베풀어요.
The boss is always generous to the employees.
잘 베풀다 = be generous/giving; describes a warm, open-handed person.
어려울 때 도움을 베풀어 주셔서 감사해요.
Thank you for extending help when times were hard.
도움을 베풀다 = extend help; more elevated and grateful than plain 도와주다.
남한테 베푼 만큼 돌아온다고 하잖아.
They say what you give to others comes back to you.
Common saying about generosity (karma-like); 만큼 = 'as much as'.
nuance: 베풀다 means to give generously of yourself — kindness, help, hospitality, favors — usually from a position of being able to give. It's warmer and more elevated than 주다, and pairs with abstract nouns (은혜, 호의, 친절, 인심) rather than concrete objects. Note the ㄹ-irregular: ㄹ drops before ㅂ/ㄴ/ㅅ (베풉니다), stays elsewhere (베풀어요, 베풀 거예요).
mistakes: Writing the formal form as 베풀습니다 — the ㄹ drops, giving 베풉니다.
Using 베풀다 with concrete gifts (선물을 베풀다 sounds odd) — pair it with abstract kindness; use 주다 for objects.

usage: 반씩 나누자
Let's split it in half
Dividing food or a bill evenly with someone; 반씩 = half each.
얘기 좀 나눠요
Let's have a chat / talk things over
이야기를 나누다 = to converse; sounds warmer and more mutual than 말하다.
examples: 피자 한 판 시켜서 친구랑 나눠 먹었어요.
I ordered a pizza and shared it with a friend.
나눠 먹다 = share food; 나누다 + 먹다 is an extremely common everyday combo.
계산은 셋이서 똑같이 나눴어요.
We split the bill evenly among the three of us.
Splitting the check (n빵/더치페이) — 나누다 is the verb for dividing the cost.
그 친구랑 고민을 나누면 마음이 편해져요.
Sharing my worries with that friend puts me at ease.
고민을 나누다 = share one's worries; 나누다 extends to feelings and conversation, not just things.
nuance: 나누다 covers two linked ideas: to divide (split a bill, cut into portions) and to share (food, feelings, conversation). The 'share' sense often appears as 나눠 먹다 (share food) and 이야기를 나누다 (have a conversation). It's warmer than a cold 'divide' — sharing with someone is the core feel. For splitting a bill specifically, 나누다 or the slang n빵 both work.
mistakes: Using 나누다 alone for 'share a post/photo online' — for social media reposting Koreans say 공유하다, not 나누다.

english: to attend on / to escort (an elder, honorific)
usage: 부모님을 모시고 살아요
I live with (and look after) my parents
모시고 살다 = live with and care for elders; 모시다 carries deep respect.
제가 모시러 갈게요
I'll come pick you up (respectfully)
Honorific version of 데리러 가다, used for a boss, client, or elder.
examples: 할아버지를 병원에 모시고 갔어요.
I took my grandfather to the hospital.
모시고 가다 = the honorific of 데리고 가다, used when accompanying an elder.
손님을 자리로 모시겠습니다.
I'll show the guest to their seat.
Set service phrase in restaurants/hotels; 모시다 elevates the customer respectfully.
사장님을 공항까지 모셔다 드렸어요.
I drove the boss to the airport.
모셔다 드리다 = escort/drive someone respectfully; standard for superiors at work.
nuance: 모시다 is the honorific verb for accompanying, escorting, taking, or living with someone of higher status — parents, grandparents, bosses, clients, guests. It replaces plain 데리고 가다/오다 (used for peers, children, pets) whenever respect is due. You'll hear it constantly in service settings ('모시겠습니다') and family talk (부모님을 모시다).
mistakes: Using 데리고 가다 for an elder or boss — that sounds rude; switch to 모시고 가다.
Using 모시다 for friends, children, or pets — it's only for people you must honor; use 데리다 otherwise.

english: to recommend / to offer / to urge
usage: 이거 한번 권해 드려요
I'd recommend trying this
Suggesting a dish or product politely; -아/어 드리다 raises it for the listener.
술을 권하다
to urge someone to drink
Pressing drinks on someone — a real (and sometimes unwelcome) part of Korean 회식 culture.
examples: 사장님이 저한테 이 메뉴를 권했어요.
The owner recommended this menu item to me.
권하다 = recommend/suggest; a touch more formal than 추천하다, often face-to-face.
어른이 술을 권하시면 두 손으로 받아요.
When an elder offers you a drink, receive it with both hands.
Key etiquette: 두 손으로 받다 = receive with both hands; essential at any 회식.
건강 생각해서 금연을 권하고 싶어요.
For your health, I'd like to urge you to quit smoking.
권하다 also = urge/advise a course of action; 금연 = quitting smoking.
nuance: 권하다 spans recommending (a dish, a book), offering (food or a drink to someone), and urging/advising (a course of action). In daily life it's strongly tied to table manners — 술을 권하다 (offering/pressing drinks) is a loaded part of 회식 culture, where refusing politely is its own skill. It's slightly more formal and personal than the neutral 추천하다.
mistakes: Assuming 권하다 always means a gentle suggestion — 술을 권하다 can mean actively pressing someone to drink, so read the context.

usage: 사양하지 말고 드세요
Don't hold back, please eat
A host urging a guest not to be polite/decline — extremely common at the table.
저는 사양할게요
I'll pass / I'll have to decline
A graceful, formal way to turn something down without sounding blunt.
examples: 마음만 받을게요. 선물은 사양할게요.
I'll accept the thought. I'll decline the gift.
Polite gift refusal; 마음만 받다 = 'I'll just take the sentiment', a set softening phrase.
한 잔 더 하라는 걸 정중히 사양했어요.
I politely declined another drink.
정중히 사양하다 = decline courteously; useful for refusing drinks at 회식 gracefully.
이런 자리는 좀 사양하고 싶어요.
I'd rather pass on gatherings like this.
사양하다 softens a refusal of an invitation/event so it doesn't feel like flat rejection.
nuance: 사양하다 is a courteous, somewhat formal way to decline an offer — food, a drink, a gift, an invitation — without the bluntness of 거절하다 (to reject). The fixed host phrase 사양하지 말고 드세요 ('don't be shy, please eat') is something you'll hear constantly at Korean tables. Because Korean politeness often involves a first refusal, knowing how to 사양하다 gracefully is genuinely useful.
mistakes: Using 거절하다 where 사양하다 fits — 거절하다 (reject) sounds firm/cold for a meal or gift; 사양하다 is the gentle, polite decline.
